limbs.label: Discrepancy shown by a held record
New: not raised and decided in 1987

rubric.mapping: Evidence only. Each limb is 0-5, times 10, and counts held records alone: 0 = no held record; 2 = held copies or photographs show it, not authenticated; 3 = a primary official record read in full shows it; 4 = an authenticated original or an expert report proves it; 5 = admissible originals ready for counsel. Inference does not score. Limbs 2 to 4 are scored only where limb 1 has a held record. Total = sum of the four limbs, 0-200. These grades are internal evidence-handling assessments, not legal findings or determinations of admissibility.
rubric.threshold_note: 100/200 is an internal research triage marker only. It is not the legal test for setting aside a judgment, a finding of dishonesty, or a prediction. Reaching it prompts a review of the underlying records with counsel; it does not establish that a case should be brought. The project’s 40/50-on-each-limb marker is an internal file-preparation checklist, not a legal test or a conclusion that evidence is admissible.
rubric.order: Score, then number of held records.
law: Takhar v Gracefield Developments Ltd [2019] UKSC 13, adopting RBS v Highland Financial Partners LP [2013] EWCA Civ 328 at [106]: a judgment can be set aside where conscious and deliberate dishonesty is proved and was an operative cause of the decision.
Lazarus Estates Ltd v Beasley [1956] 1 QB 702 (Denning LJ): a judgment obtained by deception cannot stand, once the deception is distinctly pleaded and proved.

Limitation Act 1980 s.32(1): where an action is based on the defendant's deception, or a relevant fact was deliberately concealed, time does not begin to run until the claimant has discovered it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it.

evidence_note: Every statement on this board cites a record in the evidence catalogue. 'Held' means the catalogue holds a copy that has been read. 'Pending' means the catalogue has a placeholder for a record not yet obtained, or no record at all. Nothing pending counts towards a score.
quarantine_note: Kissed-frog items are quarantined, under scrutiny, and never scored here.

rows.title: The 1939 agreement: the 'John Williams' signature against the signature

facts.t: Glamorgan Archives DBDT123/7, May 1939: an agreement between Western Ground Rents and John Williams, held as a photograph of page 2 and the plan. It carries a tenant signature 'John Williams'.
Typed terms on the photograph: a monthly let from 1 March 1939 at eight shillings a month, kept 'as meadow or pasture land'. The plan shows Parcel B (the eastern fields) only.

A inscription 'John Williams' with '1886' beneath, catalogued as a photograph on 30 October 2026 in the research mirror (not in the canonical catalogue, where EV-0902 is a different record). Recorded visible form: ornate capital J, wide letter spacing and an extended final stroke; the 1939 signature is more compact with a compressed ending.
The 1987 judgment records that John Williams 'fell into arrears with his rent in the mid-1930s and in the late 1940s'.
The 1987 judgment mentions no agreement dated 1939 and no signature. Its history runs from a February 1916 tenancy to a 1949 surrender and new tenancy.

pending.t: Page 1 of the agreement and sight of the original at Glamorgan Archives.
Known, dated signatures of John Williams, and the heirloom originals with object, date and custody recorded.
A forensic document examiner's comparison of the originals.
A record that the 1939 agreement was relied on in the 1955, 1962 or 1984–87 proceedings.

why.a: Two held images differ in visible form (EV-0023 and the research-mirror comparator). Neither is authenticated and no examiner has compared the originals.
why.b: No held record shows the 1987 court relied on the 1939 agreement; the judgment does not mention it (EV-0080).
why.c: The judgment mentions no signature (EV-0080); the comparator was catalogued on 30 October 2026 (research-mirror comparator).
why.d: Photographs only: page 1 is not held (EV-0023) and the inscription is not authenticated (research-mirror comparator).

rows.status: Held: two photographs. Pending: originals and an examiner

rows.title: 31 October 1974 licence letters: unilateral offer, repudiation and BP's knowledge

facts.t: The 1987 judgment records that WGR's 1959 tenancy offer to Mary was refused. It also recounts a further weekly-tenancy offer in 1965; the original offers and plans are needed to verify their terms and land extent.
Mary pleaded ownership in the 1974 BP Pension Trust possession proceedings; BP was a party. The Court of Appeal records that the action was never finally heard. The original pleading is not yet held.
The 31 October 1974 letters offered lifetime, rent-free occupation. The judgment records that BP neither sought nor waited for Mary's acceptance.
Her solicitor received the letters on 4 November; the judge stayed execution pending her agreement, and the warrant was withdrawn before she had given instructions.

The Court of Appeal treated the letters as a licence in the absence of repudiation and found that Mary was not asserting ownership during the period from receipt until after 11 December 1974. This was central to the result.
The Daily Telegraph report of 16 April 1974 records Mary publicly asserting a valid claim before the October letters. It does not establish a later repudiation communicated to BP.

pending.t: Any written reply, instruction or other communication in which Mary rejected the 31 October letters and maintained ownership, together with proof BP or its solicitors received it. No such post-letter communication is presently held.
The original 31 October 1974 letters, envelope, covering letter and proof of delivery to Mary's solicitor.
The original pleading, defence, witness statement and order from the 1974 county-court proceedings in which Mary asserted ownership.
The 1984–87 litigation file, including BP's witness statements, trial transcript, lists of documents and any account of Mary's post-letter position.
The original 1959 and 1965 tenancy offers, responses and plans, to verify exact wording, land extent and whether the two strands were separate.
A reported post-1974 newspaper account of Mary's renewed rejection is not yet identified by a verified title, date and page. Locate the original clipping before relying on it.

Establish whether Linklaters & Paines acted for BP in the 1974 licence episode; compare the original 1974 letters and solicitor correspondence with the firm's 1982–83 Form 1E/Form 1C submissions and examination correspondence.

why.a: The 1987 judgment establishes the unilateral offer and the court's no-repudiation finding. No held post-letter record yet contradicts that finding or proves that BP knowingly gave a false account.
why.b: The no-repudiation finding was central to the 1987 outcome. A proved, communicated repudiation or a knowingly false account of one could be directly material.
why.c: A primary record contradicting the post-letter account may be new, but no such record is currently held. The pre-letter 1974 ownership assertion does not by itself prove a later repudiation.
why.d: The judgment and 16 April 1974 press report are held. The 1974 letters, reply/instructions, pleading and BP trial evidence remain incomplete or pending.

rows.status: Unilateral licence mechanism documented; post-letter repudiation and dishonest account not proved

rows.title: 1982–83 first registration: WA231076, WA240304 and applicant disclosure

facts.t: The 1987 judgment records BP Properties as registered proprietor following first registration in November 1982. WA231076 and WA240304 were separate applications before their later amalgamation.

HMLR's 23 March 2026 history gives two dates: WA231076 applied for on 30 November 1982, relying on a 19 November 1982 BP-to-BP conveyance; WA240304 applied for on 23 February 1983, relying on a 23 May 1975 conveyance. BP Properties was applicant on both.

HMLR's 23 March 2026 letter identifies Linklaters & Paines as the solicitors who submitted both first-registration applications for BP Properties: WA231076 on 30 November 1982 and WA240304 on 23 February 1983. The 30 July schedule lists further Linklaters correspondence in both files. Whether the firm also handled the 1974 licence episode, and what it knew at each date, must be checked against its original file.

HMLR's 19 April 2026 Stage 1 letter says a 1971 abstract was lodged for WA231076 and HMLR had sight of a copy for WA240304. It quotes wording from modern Form FR1; this does not establish what the historical Forms 1E and 1C actually said in 1982–83.

HMLR's 25 May 2026 Stage 2 letter says it did not receive or know of any family interest or possible ongoing dispute at registration and no caution had been lodged. It says the applicants provided documentary title. This is HMLR's retrospective account; it does not reveal what BP answered on Form 1C or Form 1E.

Neither HMLR's 25 May response nor the 30 July inventory identifies a notice to Mary or an occupier-service record. The schedule does not name a notice item, but that does not prove none was sent; any separate notice/service record and the applicable 1983 notice rules must be obtained.
HMLR's 30 July 2026 letter confirms all listed file documents are held and open to public inspection. It lists 30 items for WA231076 and 13 for WA240304 (43 in total).

For WA231076, the schedule identifies item 13 as the Form 1E first-registration application, item 17 as the A13 list of documents lodged, item 16 as 12 May 1983 correspondence from Linklaters and Land Registry, and item 18 as an undated Linklaters letter.

For WA240304, the schedule identifies item 11 as Form 1C, item 7 as the D23 inside-exam form and Linklaters letter dated 8 April 1983, item 4 as 12 April 1983 correspondence, item 5 as undated Linklaters letters, item 10 as the first register, and items 12–13 as the May 1975 conveyance and a plan dated 23 February 1975.

The 1983 legal framework was the Land Registration Act 1925 and Rules then in force. The later 2003 Rule 28 / Form DI disclosure requirement must not be applied retrospectively. Section 14 declarations were required only if the Registrar called for them.

The Court of Appeal treated any title Mary had already acquired as capable of binding BP's registration as an overriding interest. Registration irregularity is therefore a distinct register-remedy issue; it was not the basis of the 1987 licence decision.

pending.t: Obtain WA240304 item 11: Form 1C, including every page, certificate, declaration and enclosure.
Obtain WA231076 item 13: Form 1E, and item 17: A13 list of documents lodged with first registration.
Obtain WA240304 item 7: D23 inside-exam form and Linklaters letter of 8 April 1983; item 4: 12 April 1983 correspondence; item 5: undated Linklaters letters.
Obtain WA231076 item 16: 12 May 1983 correspondence between Linklaters & Paines and HM Land Registry; item 18: undated Linklaters letter.
Obtain WA240304 item 10: the register as first made; item 12: the 23 May 1975 conveyance; item 13: the plan dated 23 February 1975. Compare the two plan dates and their land extent.
Establish whether the Registrar required any section 14 Land Registration Act 1925 affidavit or declaration. If so, obtain its exact wording, maker, date and exhibits.

Obtain any notice, enquiry or advertisement record relating to Mary or other occupiers, including the date, method, recipient and address. HMLR says no caution was lodged; that does not establish whether some other notice was prescribed.
Reconcile HMLR's statement that the 1971 abstract was lodged/sighted with the 30 July schedule, which does not list it. Its absence from the schedule alone does not prove it was never lodged.

Compare Linklaters & Paines' 1974 licence correspondence and knowledge with the firm's 1982–83 Form 1E/Form 1C submissions, D23 examination and 12 May 1983 letters. Establish whether the firm acted in both periods and what the registration team knew.

why.a: Mary's ownership claim was not hidden from BP: BP was involved in her 1974 proceedings. The narrower suspected concealment is whether the 1982–83 application package failed to reveal the disputed, unilateral nature of the purported licence or represented her occupation as settled permission, leaving HMLR unaware. The forms and any Registrar-required declaration must be read before alleging a false answer.
why.b: A proved registration mistake, false declaration or lack of proper care may support a separate rectification or indemnity route. The 1987 judgment did not rely on first registration to decide the legal effect of the 1974 letters.
why.c: The 1987 judgment records the prior ownership dispute and the legal effect later attributed to the 1974 letters. It does not determine what was said in the 1982–83 first-registration applications or whether Mary received notice. Those are separate registration and notice questions unless linked to a dishonest statement material to the 1987 outcome.
why.d: The 19 April, 25 May and 30 July HMLR PDFs are now directly read. The 30 July letter confirms 43 documents are held and open to public inspection. The underlying Forms 1C/1E, D23, A13 and correspondence still need to be obtained and assessed.

rows.status: BP knew Mary's ownership claim; question is whether the registration package concealed the disputed licence and whether Mary was notified
